newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Iraq oil deal does not mean sanctions end.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Iraq oil deal does not mean sanctions end.

text.p: The "oil-for-food deal" authorised by the United Nations on Monday does not signal the end of a tough sanctions regime against Iraq, the United States said.

"This does not signal an end or the first step toward the end of the sanctions regime against Iraq, against (President) Saddam Hussein's regime," State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters.

He spoke after the United Nations authorised the start of a long-delayed "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq, enabling Baghdad to make a limited return to the world oil market for the first time since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Under the deal, concluded in May but held up by disputes over implementation, Iraq will be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods to help offset the effects of sanctions in force for the past six years.

"We view this as a positive development," Davies said, noting that the United States had been an original sponsor of the deal. "It is and has been all along a humanitarian exception to what is a, we believe, a necessary and vigorous sanctions regime" put in place after Baghdad's invasion of Kuwait, he said.

The United States, which led the international coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War, has taken a leading role in maintaining tough sanctions on Iraq. The State Department comments on Monday were meant to offset any illusions Baghdad or others may have about an early end to the sanctions regime.
Iraq and countries with a major interest in tapping its lucrative oil market, such as France and Russia, have long been pressing for an easing, if not permanent lifting, of the sanctions.

But Washington has insisted Baghdad must go much further in meeting conditions, like disclosing the fate of Kuwaitis who went missing in the Gulf War and proving it is not trying to rebuild its programme of weapons of mass destruction.

The United States went along with the "oil for food deal" in part to help out its ally Turkey, which has been badly hurt by the sanctions against Iraq, and partly to assuage concerns that the sanctions have been hurting ordinary Iraqi civilians, not Saddam and his elite.
Washington has long argued that despite the sanctions, Saddam is spending millions of dollars on a plush lifestyle, including palaces, while allowing his people to suffer.
